title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This incident is a case of a model asserting false information as fact, specifically fabricating legal citations, case titles, quotes, and holdings that do not exist. The failure occurred at the point of output use: an attorney incorporated AI-generated text into court filings without independently verifying that the cited cases were real. The attorney believed the tool was connected to a verified legal research subscription, which means the misunderstanding about the tool's capabilities preceded any check on its output.

The failure mode is well established: a generative AI system produced plausible-looking but fictitious legal authorities, and no human verification step caught the fabrications before the filings were submitted. Seven non-existent case citations appeared across eight separate filings. Catching this would have required checking each citation against an authoritative legal database before submission, a step that is standard practice in legal work done without AI assistance.

What is not established is whether the tool itself, Irys, was marketed as citation-verified, whether State Farm directed the use of AI in these filings, or whether the court has yet imposed any sanction on counsel. The admissions reported are by the attorneys involved, not findings by the court.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, non-existent quotes, and false case holdings in their court filings. The case involves homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, whose Carson home became uninhabitable after a 2020 fire. While repairs were underway, storm damage occurred, and following delays in obtaining State Farm's approval, the work was never completed. Meni-Siliga has since lost her home to foreclosure after exhausting her savings and retirement accounts.

Attorney Jacquelene Robinson acknowledged that seven case citations across eight filings did not exist and some case titles and quotes were incorrect. She stated she used an AI tool called Irys, mistakenly believing it was connected to her law firm's legal research subscription and would verify citations. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court and plaintiff, accepting responsibility for the filings. The trial is scheduled for October, and State Farm stated it expects its external counsel to maintain the highest ethical standards and verify all legal filings accurately.
